summary: SIP networks need controls to prevent congestion collapse during overload. This document builds on a loss-based approach to remedy known weaknesses of 503 overload control and defines a rate-based control mechanism.

eli5.summary: When too many calls arrive at once, a server can tell others to slow down to a certain speed. This RFC defines how to say how many calls per second are allowed.

questions: how does sip rate based overload control work
what is the sip oc-algo parameter
subtitle: How an overloaded SIP server tells its clients the maximum number of requests per second they may send.

tldr.problem: When a SIP server is overloaded, a loss-based control scheme passes every swing in load straight through to the server, cannot guarantee an upper bound on client load, and needs frequent updates.
tldr.mechanism: The server measures its own load and tells each client a target maximum request rate in the oc parameter of the Via header field. Clients throttle new requests to that rate, for example with a leaky bucket.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a hard upper bound on the request rate that stays constant between server updates. The trade-off is more algorithmic complexity, since the server is likely to set a different target for each client.

today: RFC 7415 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an optional alternative to the default loss-based algorithm in RFC 7339.

sections.title: Why a Rate-Based Scheme
sections.content:
Large Next Generation Networks that use SIP need ways to handle traffic growth. In particular, they must handle overload gracefully and keep transaction throughput up by preventing congestion collapse.

RFC 7339 defines the signaling for SIP overload control and a default loss-based algorithm. The authors point out that a loss-based scheme is sensitive to variations in load, because any increase in load is reflected directly in the load offered to the overloaded server. It also cannot guarantee an upper bound on client load and needs frequent updates, which may affect stability.

This RFC adds a rate-based algorithm as an optional alternative. It guarantees an upper bound on the rate of requests clients send to an overloaded server, constant between server updates. The cost is algorithmic complexity, because the server is more likely to use a different target for each client.
sections.eli5: Telling people to skip some of their questions is hard to predict. Telling them a speed limit is easier, because the shopkeeper then knows the most that can ever arrive.

sections.title: How the Scheme Works
sections.content:
The server is the entity the algorithm protects, and the client is the one that throttles traffic towards it. Following the procedures of RFC 7339, they first signal each other that they support rate-based control.

The server then periodically uses internal measurements, such as CPU utilization or queueing delay, to judge its overload state and estimate a target maximum SIP request rate in requests per second. When overloaded, it puts that rate in the oc parameter of the Via header field of its SIP responses. Each client then throttles new requests towards the server.
sections.eli5: The shopkeeper checks how tired they are, picks a number of questions per second, and writes it on a note that goes back with every answer.

sections.title: Via Parameters and Algorithm Selection
sections.content:
The Via header parameters come from RFC 7339. For rate control they work like this:

  • oc: used by clients to show overload control support, and by servers to give the maximum rate in messages per second.
  • oc-algo: clients list the algorithms they support, and servers name the one in effect. Values are loss (default) and rate (optional).
  • oc-validity: how long, in milliseconds, the reduction applies. A value of 0 is reserved for the server to stop overload control, and any other case needs a non-zero value.
  • oc-seq: a sequence number tied to the oc parameter.

Clients MUST show support by including the token rate in the oc-algo list, and servers MUST show selection by setting oc-algo to rate. A client that supports only the default loss-based algorithm is handled as in Section 5.10.2 of RFC 7339.
sections.eli5: The note has little boxes: how fast, for how long, and which kind of rule is being used. Both sides must say they understand the speed-limit rule before it is used.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
How the server decides it is overloaded and estimates its target rate is outside the scope of the RFC. The server MUST, however, periodically evaluate its overload state and estimate a rate beyond which it would become overloaded. It decides how to split that rate among its clients: the same rate for each, or different rates for different clients. It MUST use the oc parameter to send each client its target.

The rate applies to the client's whole stream of requests, even if throttling only touches some of them, because request prioritization is the client's responsibility. A server may need to consider the workload of the message types a client sends, which may differ under overload restriction.

The oc value is an upper bound. Some clients may send below it and others above it at any moment, but the combined rate seen by the server will converge towards the target.
sections.eli5: The shopkeeper decides how to share out the question budget. Some people use less than their share, but together they stay near the total.

sections.title: The Client Leaky Bucket
sections.content:
A client may use any algorithm that keeps its message rate within the oc value. Define T = 1 / oc as the target interval between requests. The example algorithm, based on ITU-T I.371, is a leaky bucket: a bucket whose content drains at 1 unit per time unit and grows by T for each forwarded request.

When a request arrives, the client computes X' = X - (ta - LCT), where X is the counter after the last forwarded request and LCT is when that request was forwarded. If X' is at most the tolerance TAU, the request is forwarded, X becomes max(0, X') + T and LCT is set to the arrival time. Otherwise the request is rejected and nothing changes.

A larger TAU tolerates more deviation in the arrival spacing and allows bigger bursts. Servers with very many clients, each sending little, benefit from a smaller TAU, and servers with few busy clients from a larger one. The RFC calls TAU = 4*T a reasonable compromise.

If oc is 0 with a non-zero oc-validity, the client should reject 100% of requests to that server. If oc-validity is 0, it should stop throttling immediately. When control is first activated, the counter starts at TAU0, which is 0 or larger but no more than TAU.
sections.eli5: Picture a bucket with a small hole. Each question you send adds a bit of water, and the water drains slowly. If the bucket is too full, you must wait before sending the next question.

sections.title: Priorities and Resonance
sections.content:
Clients may sort requests into priority categories. With two categories the bucket uses two thresholds, TAU1 < TAU2. All new requests are admitted when the counter is at or below TAU1. Only higher-priority requests are admitted between TAU1 and TAU2. Everything is rejected at or above TAU2. This extends to n priorities with n thresholds. Setting both to the same value is the same as no priority. Reasonable values are TAU0 = 0, TAU1 = 1/2 * TAU2 and TAU2 = 10 * T.

As clients multiply, T grows, and the buckets of many clients can become synchronized, giving 'peaky' arrivals at the server, instability, poor delays and even lost messages. The RFC calls this resonance. An optional fix is to randomize bucket occupancy at activation and whenever the bucket empties: when X' is not above 0, pick u uniformly between -1/2 and +1/2, and on admission add T + uT instead of T. The maximum occupancy then becomes TAU + (3/2)T instead of TAU + T.
sections.eli5: Important questions can use a second, deeper line in the bucket. And if everyone starts at exactly the same moment, a little randomness stops them all from rushing in together.

sections.title: A Worked Exchange
sections.content:
The example adapts RFC 7339. Client P1 sends an INVITE to P2 with oc and oc-algo="loss,rate" in the Via header. P2 answers with oc-algo="rate" and oc-validity=0, meaning no control is active yet; oc is ignored in that case.

Later P2 becomes overloaded and replies with oc=150, oc-algo="rate" and oc-validity=1000. P1 should send requests at a rate no greater than 150 per second for 1,000 milliseconds.
sections.eli5: First both sides agree on the rule. Later the shopkeeper says: no more than 150 questions per second for the next second.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Apart from the resonance concerns above, the mechanism adds no security concerns beyond the general overload control issues in RFC 7339.

The ABNF extension is one line: algo-list =/ "rate". IANA registered the oc-algo Via parameter in the 'Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values' subregistry of the SIP Parameters registry, with predefined values and references to RFC 7339 and RFC 7415.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about, except crowds rushing in together, which the randomness trick handles. The new word rate was added to the official list.
